questions.q: Why does hardware failure become a near-certainty, rather than a rare edge case, on a large training cluster running for days or weeks?
options: GPUs manufactured for AI training are inherently less reliable than GPUs used for graphics
With hundreds or thousands of components (GPUs, NICs, nodes) each carrying some nonzero failure rate, running continuously over many GPU-hours makes at least one failure increasingly likely
Training clusters are intentionally built with unreliable hardware to reduce cost
Hardware failure is actually rare at scale and checkpointing is unnecessary in practice
questions.explain: At large scale and long duration, the sheer number of components and GPU-hours involved means the probability that at least one component fails during the run climbs sharply, even if any single component is individually reliable.

questions.q: Besides the model weights, what else must a training checkpoint capture to resume correctly?
options: Only the model architecture definition, since weights and optimizer state can be regenerated automatically
Nothing else is needed; weights alone are sufficient to resume training exactly where it left off
A complete copy of every previous checkpoint ever saved during the run
Optimizer state, the training step/epoch counter, RNG state, and the data loader's position — without these, resumed training effectively restarts key parts of the process and can destabilize
questions.explain: A checkpoint has to reproduce the full training state, not just the weights: optimizer state (e.g. Adam's moments), step/epoch counters, RNG state, and data position all matter for correct, stable resumption.

questions.q: What is the core trade-off involved in choosing how often to checkpoint during a long training run?
options: Checkpointing more often always improves training speed with no downside
Checkpoint frequency has no effect on either safety or performance
Checkpointing less often increases the progress lost on failure; checkpointing more often increases I/O overhead that can slow down training even when nothing fails
Checkpoint frequency only matters for inference workloads, not training
questions.explain: There's a genuine balance: infrequent checkpoints risk losing more GPU-hours of progress to a single failure, while frequent checkpoints add I/O overhead that can eat into training throughput if it blocks the training loop.

questions.q: What does asynchronous checkpointing specifically do to address the checkpoint-frequency trade-off?
options: It eliminates the need to ever save optimizer state
It writes checkpoint data to fast local/host memory first and lets training continue immediately, flushing to durable storage in the background rather than blocking on the full write
It saves checkpoints only once, at the very end of training, regardless of duration
It requires training to pause completely until the checkpoint write to durable storage finishes
questions.explain: Asynchronous checkpointing decouples the slow durable-storage write from the training critical path, letting teams checkpoint more frequently without paying the full I/O cost in blocked GPU time on every checkpoint.

questions.q: How does checkpoint interval map onto the RPO/RTO language from this path's resilience and disaster-recovery content?
options: Checkpoint interval corresponds to RPO (maximum acceptable progress loss); the time to detect a failure and resume from the last checkpoint corresponds to RTO (maximum acceptable downtime)
RPO and RTO apply only to databases and have no meaningful equivalent in model training
Checkpoint interval corresponds to RTO, and the number of GPUs corresponds to RPO
RPO and RTO are interchangeable terms that both refer to the total length of the training run
questions.explain: A checkpoint interval of 30 minutes caps progress loss at 30 minutes on any single failure — that's the training-job equivalent of RPO. How long it takes to detect the failure, restart, and reload the checkpoint is the training-job equivalent of RTO.
